title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself — your name, where you are from, which languages you speak — and ask others the same.
intro: In this unit you meet the Tamil pronouns, which come in polite and intimate versions, and learn that Tamil usually needs **no verb 'to be'** to say who or what someone is: நான் அன்னா 'I (am) Anna'. You will also meet the main question words and the handy question suffix **-ஆ** *-ā*.

vocab.note: spoken: அவரு avaru (mostly for men); for a woman, polite அவங்க avanga
spoken: நாம nāma; also நம்ம namma 'our'
spoken: ஊரு ūru. உங்க ஊரு எது? = 'Where are you from?'

vocab.en: be (somewhere / in a state); stay; exist
vocab.note: spoken present: இருக்கேன் irukkēn 'I am', இருக்கு irukku 'it is / there is'
dative subject: எனக்குத் தெரியும் 'I know'; negative தெரியாது teriyādu

phrases.en: Where are you from? (lit. you which town?)
I'm from London. (lit. I come from London)
I live in Chennai now. (lit. I am in Chennai)
I speak a little bit of Tamil.
Nice to meet you. (lit. happiness in seeing you)

grammar.title: Pronouns and levels of respect
grammar.body:
Tamil pronouns encode **respect**. For 'he/she' there are three levels:

**அவன்** *avan* — he (boy, friend, someone younger)
**அவ** *ava* (written அவள்) — she (girl, friend, someone younger)
**அவரு** *avaru* (written அவர்) — he/she, respectful
**அவங்க** *avanga* (written அவர்கள்) — they; also a very respectful he/she, especially for women
**அது** *adu* — it (animals, things; also a baby)

So talking about your teacher, you say அவரு or அவங்க, never அவன்/அவ. 'We' also has two forms: **நாம** (written நாம், *we including you*) and **நாங்க** (*we, but not you*). The near-forms start with **இ-** instead of **அ-**: இவரு 'this person (here)', இவங்க, இது.

grammar.title: 'X is Y' needs no verb — but 'being somewhere' uses இரு
grammar.body:
To say what or who someone **is**, just put the two nouns side by side: **நான் அன்னா** 'I (am) Anna', **இது தமிழ்** 'this (is) Tamil'. There is no word for 'am/is/are' in these sentences.

To say where someone **is**, or how they **are**, use the verb **இரு** *iru* 'to be, stay'. Its spoken present tense:

நான் இருக்கேன் *irukkēn* — I am
நீ இருக்க *irukka* — you are (informal)
நீங்க இருக்கீங்க *irukkīnga* — you are (polite)
அவன் இருக்கான் *irukkān* / அவ இருக்கா *irukkā* — he / she is
அவரு இருக்காரு *irukkāru* / அவங்க இருக்காங்க *irukkānga* — he/she (resp.), they are
நாங்க / நாம இருக்கோம் *irukkōm* — we are
அது இருக்கு *irukku* — it is; there is

grammar.title: Question words and the question suffix -ஆ
grammar.body:
Tamil question words mostly start with **எ-** *e-*: என்ன 'what', எங்க 'where', எப்போ 'when', எப்படி 'how', எது 'which', எந்த 'which (+ noun)', plus யாரு 'who' and ஏன் 'why'. They stay in the place where the answer would go — no moving to the front.

For **yes/no questions**, add **-ஆ** *-ā* to the end of the word you are asking about (usually the verb), with rising pitch: தெரியும் 'know' → தெரியுமா? 'do you know?'. After a consonant or certain vowels a glide appears: தமிழ் → தமிழா? *tamiḻā*, சரி → சரியா? *sariyā*.

examples.en: Where are you? / Where do you live?

dialogue.title: On the train to Madurai
dialogue.setting: Tom, a British traveller, gets talking to a young woman, Priya, on the train.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: கொஞ்சம் கொஞ்சம் தெரியும். என் பேரு டாம். உங்க பேரு என்ன?
lines.roman: konjam konjam teriyum. en pēru Ṭām. unga pēru enna?
lines.en: Just a little. My name is Tom. What's your name?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: My name is Priya. I'm from Madurai.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: I live in Chennai. He's my elder brother.

culture: Asking 'which town are you from?' (எந்த ஊரு?) is one of the first questions Tamils ask, since one's native place (சொந்த ஊரு) matters a lot even for city-dwellers. Many Tamils use only a given name plus an initial (the father's name), e.g. 'R. Priya'. Mixing English words into Tamil ('Tanglish') is completely normal in cities — don't be surprised to hear 'office', 'bus', 'phone' in every sentence.
